records.mechanism: Tokenization splits on whitespace (re.split(r'\s+', ...)) and then relies on word.strip(string.punctuation) to clean edges, instead of the canonical re.split(r'\W+', ...) which splits on every run of non-word characters. Whitespace-splitting keeps two words joined by internal punctuation (no space) as a single token, and strip() only removes punctuation at the ENDS, so the internal separator survives and the pair is counted as one word.

records.mechanism: Instead of Counter(urls).most_common(top_n), the top-N is computed as sorted(counts.items(), key=count-ascending)[-top_n:]. Python's sort is stable, so among URLs tied on the same count this ascending-then-take-last idiom preserves the LAST-inserted tied elements, whereas most_common keeps the FIRST-inserted ones. When there are more than top_n unique URLs and a tie straddles the cut-off, a different subset is returned.

records.mechanism: The JSON is parsed with an object_pairs_hook (merge_pairs) that resolves duplicate object keys by keeping the FIRST occurrence (`if key not in obj`). Standard json.loads (used by the canonical) resolves duplicate keys with LAST-wins semantics. So when a JSON object contains a repeated key, this version reads the shadowed earlier value instead of the effective final value.

records.mechanism: The canonical uses re.search to grab the FIRST timestamp per log line (the leading log timestamp). This version uses re.finditer and loops over EVERY HH:MM:SS pattern in an ERROR line, appending each to error_times and into the average. It only diverges when an ERROR message body itself contains a time-like substring (e.g. 'will retry at 10:30:00'), in which case it records a phantom error occurrence.

records.mechanism: The average is divided by error_count (every line containing 'ERROR') instead of len(error_times) (only the errors that had a parseable timestamp). Faithful draw: json.dumps({'text': <prose>}) where prose is 0-9 space-joined tokens of ordinary words plus occasional all-punctuation tokens. Ordinary prose whitespace only (space) - exotic control whitespace such as \f/\v is not part of realistic text.
records.spec_verdict_note: Trigger region is effectively measure-zero under a spec-faithful input distribution. No blind fuzzing budget reaches it.
records.mechanism: The cleaning regex character class enumerates the allowed whitespace explicitly as `[^a-zA-Z0-9 \t\n\r]` instead of the canonical `[^\sa-zA-Z0-9]` which uses `\s`. This looks identical for ordinary text but silently omits the exotic ASCII whitespace characters form feed (\x0c) and vertical tab (\x0b) (and unicode whitespace). Those characters are therefore DELETED rather than preserved as separators. When two words are separated only by a form feed, they get glued together into one token before `.split()` runs, so the two distinct words are merged and their counts are wrong.

records.mechanism: This implementation splits the text into tokens FIRST, then strips non-alphanumeric characters from each token individually. It forgets to skip tokens that become empty after cleaning. When a whitespace-delimited token consists entirely of punctuation (e.g. a standalone '&', '-', '/'), the cleaning step reduces it to the empty string '', which is then incremented in the counter, producing a spurious '' key. The canonical solution removes punctuation across the whole string before splitting, so all-punctuation runs simply vanish and never become a token.

records.mechanism: Counts matches as len(re.split(pattern, string)) - 1. For patterns with no capturing groups this equals the number of non-overlapping matches, matching the canonical exactly. But re.split inserts the text of any capturing groups into the returned list, so when a pattern contains a group the piece count is inflated and the reported match count is too high.
